displayQuote: I cannot teach anybody anything, I can only make them think

meta.title: Who really said "I cannot teach anybody anything, I can only make them think"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Unsourced. Socrates wrote nothing, and this sentence is in none of the four ancient sources for him. But it compresses something he really does say — in Plato's Theaetetus and Apology, almost word for word in substance.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I cannot teach anybody anything, I can only make them think'?
meta.ogDescription: No ancient source — but an unusually honest fake. Plato's Socrates calls himself a midwife who is barren of wisdom, and says outright that his companions 'never learned anything from me.'

answer.label: Unsourced — a modern summary of a real Socratic claim
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · modern English paraphrase, no located first use
answer.sourceLine: No ancient text says this. Socrates wrote nothing, so the whole record of him is Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Aristotle — and the sentence is in none of them. It is a modern English compression, endlessly reproduced without a citation. What makes it unusual is that the compression is fair: Plato’s Socrates really does deny being a teacher, and really does claim he only delivers other people’s thoughts. The genuine wording is on this page.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Well, my art of midwifery is in most respects like theirs; but differs, in that I attend men and not women; and look after their souls when they are in labour, and not after their bodies… And like the midwives, I am barren, and the reproach which is often made against me, that I ask questions of others and have not the wit to answer them myself, is very just… It is quite clear that they never learned anything from me; the many fine discoveries to which they cling are of their own making.
trail: The decisive point first: Socrates published nothing, so everything we have about him is second-hand — Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes or Aristotle the second-hand record ↗. This sentence is in none of them: no Greek sentence anywhere in the corpus corresponds to it, and it appears in none of the standard English translations we searched — Jowett’s Theaetetus and Apology, linked below.

It also behaves like a modern saying. It appears on quotation aggregators with no work, no section, no translator; the punctuation drifts between a comma and a full stop; and there is no Greek text anywhere upstream of it. Quotations with a real dialogue behind them do not lose their citation this completely.

But the idea is genuinely his. In the Theaetetus Socrates describes himself as a midwife who is himself barren of wisdom, delivering other men of their own thoughts and testing whether each newborn idea is ‘a false idol or a noble and true birth’ — then says flatly that his companions ‘never learned anything from me’ Theaetetus, Jowett ↗.

The Apology puts it even more bluntly, on trial for his life: ‘Not that I have any regular disciples… for I never taught or professed to teach him anything.’ Denying that he was a teacher was, at that moment, a legal defence as well as a philosophical position Apology, Jowett ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the real passage, not the quote. Notice how much odder it is than the slogan. Socrates does not say he prefers to make people think; he says he is barren, that the god forbids him to give birth to ideas of his own, and that the reproach of asking questions he cannot answer is entirely just. The modern line keeps the method and quietly drops the humiliation.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be given for the quotation itself: it is modern, anonymous and untraced, and an unknown author is not a dead one. Do not treat it as free stock text. Everything we quote from Plato here is clear — Benjamin Jowett’s Victorian translations of the Theaetetus and the Apology are long out of copyright, and Jowett is the safest Socrates to reproduce for that reason. Modern translations (Cornford, Grube, Rowe) are not. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Socrates
author.metaLine: c. 470–399 BC · Athenian philosopher, as portrayed by Plato and Xenophon
author.bio: Socrates spent his life asking questions he claimed not to be able to answer, and this saying is the tidy version of that. It gets credited to him for the best possible reason — it is roughly true — and that is what makes it durable. He is the patron saint of every teacher who has ever refused to lecture, and the line is quoted in staffrooms and keynote slides as a licence. The real Socrates is a harsher patron than that: he compared himself to a stinging gadfly, insisted he was barren of wisdom, and was executed by the city he questioned.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the gentlest kind of misattribution: a fair summary that has been promoted to a quotation. It still fails, because a paraphrase in quotation marks is a claim about a document, and here there is no document.

items.why: Socrates wrote nothing; the record is Plato, Xenophon, Aristophanes and Aristotle; the sentence is in none of them. Nobody who reproduces it names a dialogue, because there is not one to name.

Socrates says his art is midwifery of the soul, that he is barren himself, and that those who improve under him ‘never learned anything from me — the many fine discoveries to which they cling are of their own making.’ That is the claim the slogan is compressing Theaetetus ↗.

‘Not that I have any regular disciples… for I never taught or professed to teach him anything.’ Said at his trial, where the distinction between teaching the young and merely talking to them was a matter of life and death Apology ↗.

The Meno’s slave-boy demonstration is often cited as the source of this line. It is a different and much stranger claim — that learning is the soul remembering what it already knew — not a modest remark about teaching style.

misattribution.truthLine: Unsourced: Socrates wrote nothing, and this sentence is in none of the four ancient sources. But Plato’s Socrates really does say his companions ‘never learned anything from me’ Theaetetus 150 ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Every teacher who has ever watched a class go quiet at the sound of an answer wants this to be real. It converts the most frustrating part of the job — not being able to hand knowledge over — into a philosophy, and gives it the oldest signature in the trade.

The genuine material is better and less comfortable. Socrates does not describe a technique; he describes a disability. He is barren, the god will not let him give birth, and the best he can do is attend other people’s labour and check whether what arrives is worth keeping.
context.detailsSummary: What Socrates actually says about teaching
detailsBody: Theaetetus 150: his art is midwifery of the soul — he attends men in labour and tests whether the thought born is a false idol or a true birth.
Theaetetus 150, again: ‘It is quite clear that they never learned anything from me.’
Apology 33: ‘Not that I have any regular disciples… for I never taught or professed to teach him anything.’
Apology 19–20: he separates himself from the Sophists, who took fees for instruction; his point is partly that he sells nothing.
Meno: the slave-boy is walked to a geometrical truth by questioning alone — the demonstration behind the whole idea.
context.pull: He does not call it a method. He calls himself barren, and says so as a confession.
